quick_notes.title: Simple Interest (SI)
quick_notes.detail: SI : (P*R*T)/100. Interest is constant every year.
quick_notes.explanation: Simple Interest (SI) is a method of calculating the extra money you pay for borrowing money or earn for lending money. The formula to find Simple Interest is SI equals (P multiplied by R multiplied by T) divided by 100, where P stands for Principal, which is the original amount of money borrowed or lent; R stands for Rate of interest per year, which is the percentage charged or earned; and T stands for Time, which is the number of years the money is borrowed or lent. For example, if you borrow 1000 rupees (the Principal) at a Rate of 10 percent per year for 3 years (the Time), the Simple Interest is (1000 times 10 times 3) divided by 100, which equals 300 rupees. The key feature of Simple Interest is that the interest amount is constant every year, meaning you pay or earn the same amount of interest each year for the entire duration. So in the example, you would pay 100 rupees in interest each year for 3 years, totaling 300 rupees.

quick_notes.title: Compound Interest (CI)
quick_notes.detail: Interest on Interest. Amount : P(1+R/100)^T. CI : Amount - P.
quick_notes.explanation: Compound Interest (CI) is the interest you earn not only on your original money but also on the interest that money has already earned, which is why it is called "interest on interest." The total amount you have after a certain time is found using the formula Amount equals P multiplied by (1 plus R divided by 100) raised to the power T, where P is the principal (the original sum of money you start with), R is the rate of interest per year (given as a percentage), and T is the time in years. To find just the Compound Interest (CI), you subtract the original principal (P) from the total Amount. For example, if you invest 100 rupees at 10% per year for 2 years, the Amount is 100 times (1 plus 10/100) squared, which equals 121 rupees, so the CI is 121 minus 100, which is 21 rupees. This is different from Simple Interest, where you only earn interest on the original 100 rupees each year.

quick_notes.title: Difference between CI & SI
quick_notes.detail: For 2 years: Diff : P(R/100)^2. For 3 years: Diff : PR^2(300+R) / 100^3.
quick_notes.explanation: The difference between Compound Interest (CI) and Simple Interest (SI) is the extra money earned because CI also earns interest on previously earned interest, while SI only earns interest on the original amount. The original amount you start with is called the Principal (P), and the percentage you earn each year is the Rate of interest (R) per annum, written as a number (not a percent). For a period of 2 years, the difference between CI and SI is calculated using the formula P times (R divided by 100) squared, which is written as P(R/100)^2. For a period of 3 years, the difference is P times R squared times (300 plus R) all divided by 100 cubed, written as PR^2(300+R) / 100^3. These formulas assume the interest is compounded once per year, meaning the interest is added to the principal at the end of each year. Use these formulas directly to find the difference when you know the principal and the rate.

quick_notes.title: Successive Method for CI
quick_notes.detail: Use x + y + (xy/100) for effective rate. (e.g., 10% for 2 yrs : 21%).
quick_notes.explanation: The Successive Method for Compound Interest (CI) helps you find the total interest rate after two or more years when the rate changes each year or is the same. Compound Interest is interest calculated on both the original amount and the interest already earned. The effective rate is the single percentage that represents the total growth over the whole period. Use the formula x + y + (xy/100), where x is the first year's percentage rate and y is the second year's percentage rate. For example, if the rate is 10% for each of two years, the effective rate is 10 + 10 + (1010/100) = 21%, meaning the total increase after two years is 21% of the original amount, not just 20%.

quick_notes.title: Half-Yearly & Quarterly
quick_notes.explanation: Here is a clear and complete mini-lesson on Half-Yearly and Quarterly reports. The Half-Yearly report, also called R/2, is a report that must be submitted once every six months, and it covers a period of two terms. The Quarterly report, also called R/4, is a report that must be submitted once every three months, and it covers a period of four terms. In these labels, the letter "R" stands for "Report," and the number after the slash tells you how many terms are in that reporting period. A "term" is a fixed unit of time, like a month or a quarter, that is used to measure how long the report covers.
